Meeting header:
Date: 2025-11-05
Time: 15:30 UTC (62 minutes)
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (Sapphire), Sara Kim (Sapphire), Nina Alvarez (Sapphire)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be fuzzy):
We ran through runtime tradeoffs for Llama/Mistral/Qwen, focused on RoPE scaling effects, MoE token routing cost, and quantization tradeoffs for on-prem vs VPC deployments. Action items: Redwood to run 8k seq benchmarks, share bench CSV; customer to assemble prompts and confirm tail-latency SLOs.

Topics: rope scaling, moe routing costs, batching + KV cache, quantization (4-bit/GPTQ/AWQ), on-prem VPC considerations, tail-latency vs throughput tradeoffs.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: okay, uh hi everyone, thanks for joining, we, um, we planned this as a deep-dive on runtime and architecture specific tuning, so Ravi and I will jump in. Can you just quick intro?
[00:12] Liam: yeah, Liam O'Connor, ML eng, running the inference stack for search and document-summarization pipelines. We're hitting tail-latency spikes at ~1% p99 when seq length goes above 4k.
[00:22] Sara: Sara Kim, infra, we'll be running pilot in our GCP VPC then maybe on-prem later. Concerned about KMS and network egress.
[00:30] Nina: Nina Alvarez, CTO, high level: cost and predictable SLAs are top priorities.
[00:36] Ravi: cool, thanks. Quick agenda: rope scaling behavior differences, MoE token routing cost patterns, batching and KV cache best practices, quantization caveats per model family, and mapping to VPC/on-prem constraints.
[01:05] Maya: first, quick sanity check, which model families are you evaluating? Liam: Llama-70b as higher-accuracy baseline, Mistral-7B variants for cost, and Qwen-14B for multi-turn dialogue. We also looked at a tiny MoE prototype for experiments — about 32 experts.
[01:28] Ravi: good. On RoPE scaling, a lot of behaviour is driven by the positional embedding implementation. Llama-style RoPE shows degradation at long contexts if you don't adjust the frequency decay; Mistral has a slightly different rotary base which tends to be stable up to 8k in our infra tests, Qwen we saw some drift, maybe due to tokenization interactions.
[01:55] Liam: can you unpack "frequency decay" — like tuneable parameter?
[02:01] Ravi: yeah so RoPE uses rotation frequency. When you scale sequence length, the effective phase can wrap and you start losing relative position signal; teams offset by scaling the base or applying rope scaling tricks (linear scaling, ALiBi-like wrappers). In practice, we saw simple linear rescaling + KV-cache-aware prefix adjustments helped maintain coherence for Llama at 8k.
[02:34] Sara: when you say KV-cache-aware, do you mean cache invalidation or physical layout? We're concerned about memory on dedicated nodes.
[02:41] Ravi: both. Two parts: 1) keep prefix/key-value segmentation to avoid copying the entire cache for every request — continuous chunked KV windowing; 2) use memory-friendly layout (bfloat16/float16) if accuracy allows. Also caching policy: prefer prefix caching for system prompts and frequently recurring contexts.
[03:00] Maya: note — customers sometimes see transcriptions saying "K V cash" in old notes, that's just speech-to-text.
[03:07] Liam: hah, we saw that. ok, MoE stuff — what's the cost shape?
[03:12] Ravi: MoE routing costs are tricky: gating introduces an additional per-token compute step and sparse-expert dispatch overhead. In practice, token routing costs roughly add 10-30% overhead on top of dense compute, but that depends on expert size, top-k gating, and hardware topology. If your batch has many short sequences, the dispatch becomes less efficient and overhead rises.
[03:40] Nina: does the routing cost dominate network for on-prem clusters?
[03:45] Ravi: It can. If experts are sharded across devices, you'll get cross-device all-to-all communication. For on-prem racks with limited NIC, that can be the bottleneck. We recommend colocating routing and top-expert shards or using kernel fusion to reduce copies. For Dedicated/Rack deployments we can pin experts to GPUs to limit cross-host traffic.
[04:10] Liam: what about dynamic capacity — overflow when expert capacity is exceeded?
[04:15] Ravi: good question. You either implement capacity factoring (extra capacity per expert) or fall back to local expert routing. Both have tradeoffs: capacity factoring increases FLOPs but reduces tail-latency; fallback reduces compute but can increase variance in quality. We usually suggest measuring the routing rejection rate on a representative workload.
[04:38] Sara: can Redwood route to a dense fallback model automatically?
[04:41] Maya: yes, we have routing policies: canary to dense fallback with configurable threshold. That is a common pattern for graceful degradation.
[04:49] [05:00] Speaker 1 (auto): note — referenced bench: drive.redwood/benchmarks/sapphire-20251105.csv
[05:08] Liam: quantization — we're trying to get costs down. Which quant libs do you recommend? GPTQ? AWQ? nf4?
[05:15] Ravi: our notes: AWQ tends to preserve generative quality for decoder-only models at 4-bit in many cases, but for some Llama variants GPTQ is still competitive. nf4 (normal float4) is good for transformers with specific numeric ranges, but it's model dependent. We also caution about KV cache fidelity: some Q4 formats slightly degrade cached key consistency — leading to small hallucination drift over long contexts.
[05:42] Maya: does Redwood test quantized model end-to-end with continuous batching + KV cache?
[05:46] Ravi: yes, we run integrated runs: quantize, then measure token-level perplexity drift over long prefixes, then measure latency/throughput with KV cache warmed. For instance, our internal 4-bit AWQ run on Mistral showed ~1.8x speedup on GPU kernels with <1.5% delta in BLEU/ROUGE-like metrics on summarization sets.
[06:12] Liam: interesting — can you share that CSV?
[06:15] Maya: we'll share the benchmark CSV in the drive link.
[06:18] Sara: networking — for VPC, how does KMS and key rotation interplay with on-prem use? We have strict HSM requirements.
[06:25] Ravi: Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS and in some cases HSM-backed keys. For on-prem we can integrate with local HSM appliances. The main thing is to ensure model weights at rest are encrypted and black-boxed; also ensure audit logs for key usage.
[06:42] Nina: what's the recommended Dedicated sizing if we want 300 QPS at median 30 tokens per request with p99 < 250ms?
[06:49] Ravi: quick back-of-envelope: depends on model and batching. For Mistral-7B quantized to 4-bit with aggressive batching and KV cache, probably 8 GPUs in a dedicated pool with continuous batching heuristics; Llama-70b dense needs more — 24+ A100-class GPUs or equivalent, or use sharded sequence parallel. We'll put a more exact Dedicated worksheet in the follow-ups.
[07:18] Liam: tail-latency mitigation — do you recommend pre-warming KV caches for user sessions?
[07:24] Ravi: yes pre-warm and sticky routing. Also use adaptive batching: when p99 climbs, temporarily reduce batch windows and shift to lower-latency model variant.
[07:40] Sara: do you have perf knobs we can tune in the private runtime? For example: batch size, batch timeout, KV evict policy, quant kernel flags?
[07:49] Ravi: yes, the runtime exposes batch_max_tokens, batch_timeout_ms, kv_window_size, kv_eviction_policy, and a quant_profile that toggles kernel selection (e.g., Q4_K_M optimized kernels). We'll share recommended starting configs per model.
[08:05] [08:30] Maya: I want to flag a common gotcha: "rope scaling" patches that superficially improve long-context can break short-context calibration. So test across your entire prompt distribution.
[08:42] Liam: do you have a simple experiment design to validate rope changes?
[08:46] Ravi: run a sliding-window perplexity vs reference for lengths 512/2k/4k/8k, and evaluate task-specific metrics (e.g., summarization ROUGE). Also run knn-detect to see if attention patterns degrade. We can provide a small harness.
[09:10] Nina: about MoE — is it realistic to consider an MoE variant for production if we want predictable SLAs?
[09:17] Ravi: yes but with caveats. For stable SLAs, you need either overprovisioned expert capacity or a deterministic fallback plan. MoE is great for cost/quality when average load has long coherent sequences, but for many short user interactions, the routing overhead and variance can make SLAs harder.
[09:40] Liam: in your internal tests did you see gating-induced p99 spikes?
[09:45] Ravi: sometimes — especially when gating concentrates tokens on a few experts — you get localized hot-spots. Techniques: increase top-k gating to spread load, or adaptive capacity. Also monitor per-expert queue lengths; Redwood console can expose that metric.
[10:05] Sara: any special kernel recommendations for Qwen? We saw a previous note where rotary implementations differ.
[10:12] Ravi: Qwen's rotary parameters mean some kernels that assume standard RoPE scaling need adjustments. We ship multiple kernel variants and pick at load-time; on some GPUs a fused rotary+matmul kernel gave 20% lower latency. We'll test Qwen-specific kernels in the bench run.
[10:35] [11:00] Speaker 2 (auto): question list captured: 1) bench CSV 2) Dedicated sizing 3) security docs 4) kernel configs
[11:08] Maya: ok let's talk about batching. If you have mostly short queries, larger batch windows harm tail latencies — but improve throughput. We recommend adaptive batching with a small max wait time and token-based batch caps. Example: batch_max_tokens = 4096, batch_timeout_ms = 6 for chat workloads; for long context generation use higher timeout.
[11:40] Liam: continuous batching + KV cache - does it interact poorly with quantized kernels?
[11:45] Ravi: sometimes. When kernels use int8 or 4-bit accumulators, fused kernels help keep consistent numerics. But some quantized kernels don't support efficient incremental KV updates, so you need a fallback path. We'll mark kernels that support continuous KV update in the worksheet.
[12:03] Sara: for on-prem, NIC considerations — should we go 100Gbps or 200Gbps for MoE experiments?
[12:10] Ravi: if you plan cross-host expert sharding and >32 experts, 200Gbps is safer. If you pin experts per host and can accept extra GPU headroom, 100Gbps might suffice. Depends on your network fabric and expected cross-host traffic.
[12:30] Nina: any gotchas on tokenization differences across models? We saw Qwen sometimes produces different token counts for the same text vs Llama.
[12:37] Ravi: yes tokenization differences change effective sequence length which impacts batching and KV sizes. Normalize by preprocessing steps or measure token-exact distribution per model before capacity planning.
[12:50] Liam: curious: what's the observed energy/cost delta between dense Llama-70b and MoE 32-expert variant with equivalent quality?
[12:57] Ravi: ballpark: MoE can reduce costs 2x on average for tasks it specializes in, but operational overhead and variability may cut that advantage. We usually model both compute and network costs in TCO. We'll include a TCO comparator in the spreadsheet.
[13:20] Maya: quick demo request: would you prefer we run the bench on Redwood Hosted or on your VPC?
[13:26] Liam: for initial numbers hosted is fine, but we want an on-prem replica for final production numbers because our NIC and HSMs matter.
[13:32] Ravi: understood. We'll run initial on Hosted and then replicate on a VPC/private cluster.
[13:40] [14:00] Speaker 1 (auto): reference doc: redwood.com/docs/private/vpc-playbook (exported)
[14:08] Sara: how about monitoring — do you provide per-token cost breakdown and per-route dashboards?
[14:14] Maya: yes console exposes token-level cost, per-model breakdown, per-route tail-latency charts and per-expert metrics for MoE. Also tracing hooks for request attribution.
[14:30] Liam: what's your recommended QC for quantized models — how much human eval?
[14:34] Ravi: we do both automated metrics and human eval — for production, sample 500 prompts for human A/B vs baseline after quantization and ensure acceptability thresholds. Also maintain regression alarms on eval prompts.
[14:52] Nina: security again — we need SOC2 + audit logs for KMS usage. Is that standard?
[14:58] Maya: Redwood has SOC2, and audit logging is part of Private and Dedicated packages. We'll attach the SOC2 doc.
[15:12] Liam: small nit — earlier you mentioned "rope linear rescaling" — is there a recommended code patch or is it model side?
[15:19] Ravi: both. There are small model-side patches (rescale position frequencies at inference time) and runtime flags to emulate. We'll share a small patch and also test it in our bench harness to show tradeoffs.
[15:38] Sara: do you support HSM-backed KMS for on-prem with automatic rotation?
[15:43] Maya: yes, with some setup steps. We'll pair engineering for that.
[15:50] [16:30] Speaker 2 (auto): capturing follow-ups: bench, security docs, Dedicated worksheet, pilot schedule
[16:40] Maya: ok let's confirm next steps — Ravi runs bench, Maya sends docs, Liam assemble prompts, Sara schedules infra kickoff. Anything else?
[16:50] Nina: also can you include example gating configs for MoE?
[16:55] Ravi: yes will include sample gating topology and capacity-factor defaults.
[17:02] Liam: one last question on quant kernels: are there GPU-specific kernel flags we should enable for L4/RTX deployments?
[17:09] Ravi: yes, some of the fused kernels depend on sm version and cuda/cuDNN builds; we'll include a compatibility matrix. For consumer GPUs we typically recommend different kernel builds.
[17:26] Maya: great. wraps up — thanks everyone.
